chapter_theme: Various ways (பன்னெறி): a closing miscellany of the Book of Wealth. It weighs the wife as what makes a house a home or a ruin, ranks the lives a person may lead with austerity first, and observes that sons inherit their fathers' minds, that the world turns upside down, and that the unfeeling are better dead.
structure_note: The quatrains fall into loose groups: the wife and household life (361-364), two ranked lists of lives, best, middle and worst (365, 366), and single observations (367-369). 370, on the courtesans' love, is almost a twin of 371 and leads into the Book of Love.

361.reading: What use is a mansion where the clouds play, under fine guard, with jewels shining like lamps, if its owner has no admirable wife? That house is a wilderness too grim to look at.
361.nuance: Pope's 'hard to explore' reads காண்டற்கு அரிய as a trackless waste; Mudaliar reads it as a forest too harsh even to look at. Shanmuganar takes இழைவிளக்கு as a wick lamp that never goes out, where Mudaliar has jewels shining like lamps.

362.reading: Even when women are kept under a faultless guard of swords, the time in which soft-spoken women commit no fault is short and the time in which they don't keep to good conduct is long; the verse's condition on this is disputed.
362.nuance: This is one of the collection's harshest lines on women, and its scope depends on the condition in the second line. Mudaliar cites Kural 57 with it, though 57 praises women's own guard rather than doubting it.

positions.position: He reads the condition as 'even if they get no chance to stray': strict guard can stop the deed, but most women's minds still go astray.
He keeps the condition as written: the claim applies if women take the faulty way.

363.reading: The wife who stands up to her husband saying 'strike me' is Death; the one who doesn't go into the kitchen at dawn is an incurable disease; the one who doesn't serve the food she has cooked is a demon in the house; these three are weapons that kill the man who took them.
363.nuance: Pope's 'gives no alms' makes the third fault a failure of charity. Both commentators make it a failure to serve the husband, and Mudaliar adds that she eats the food herself.

364.reading: He hears marriage called a dread and doesn't give it up; he hears the funeral drum beat loud enough to split heads and still doesn't see; to take a wife again and live lost in pleasure, they say, is the fault of stoning oneself.
364.nuance: Shanmuganar places the drum at the first wife's funeral, which makes this a verse about remarriage. Mudaliar points back to quatrain 56, where கடி names marriage as something to be dreaded. On either reading the verse goes further than a warning about remarrying: it treats household life itself as what the wise tell one to give up.

365.reading: The best way to live is to strive in austerity; the middle way is to dwell with those one loves; the lowest is to follow, out of desire for wealth, people who don't recognise one's worth, even thinking it won't come.
365.nuance: இனியார் is general, 'the dear ones', and both commentators narrow it to wives. Mudaliar reads புணராது என்று எண்ணி as 'even while thinking it won't be gained', which makes the lowest life futile as well as servile; Pope's 'not enough' reads it as discontent.

366.reading: The best pass their time in learning, the middle in enjoying good things, and the lowest lie sleepless with resentment, saying 'we haven't eaten well, we haven't got enough'.
366.nuance: கல்லா here means 'having learned', not 'not learning'. Mudaliar specifies books of spiritual knowledge and goods gained by right means; the verse says only learning and good things. The lowest are marked by craving rather than by poverty.

367.reading: Lord of the rich-fielded town where the paddy fills the fields: since the sprout from red paddy grows again into that same red paddy, a son's understanding is his father's.
367.nuance: The verse states inheritance as a law, the way a seed breeds true. It doesn't say whether the son learns from his father or is born like him. Mudaliar's parallel, 'the son tells the father's worth', reads the son as the sign of his lineage.

368.reading: The wealthy of long standing and the worthy decline, while concubines' sons and base men flourish; what belongs at the feet comes to the head, and like an umbrella's handle the world stands upside down.
368.nuance: Shanmuganar explains the umbrella: its handle points down when the umbrella is open and up when it is folded, so the same world can flip between orders. The complaint mixes moral and social rank, putting the worthy beside old wealth and the base beside concubines' sons.

369.reading: Lord of the good land of mighty hills, whose falls sweep down gems: those whose hearts don't ease the pain their dear ones tell them of would do better to leap from a cliff than to live.
369.nuance: The verse doesn't require them to remove the pain, only to be moved by it; a heart unmoved disqualifies a life. Mudaliar takes இனியார் as friends.

370.reading: Fresh floodwater and the friendship of women with fine earrings, examined calmly, are no different: the flood ends when the rain ends, and their love ends when the income ends.
370.nuance: Mudaliar records a second reading of விதுப்பு அற, 'without desire', which would make the examiner a man no longer infatuated.

links.note: 53 asks what is lacking if the wife has worth and what is present if she lacks it. 361 gives the second half a picture: every grandeur present, and the house a wilderness.
Both say guards can't keep women chaste. 57 concludes that a woman's own steadfastness is the best guard; 362, on Mudaliar's reading, doubts that most women have it.
52 says a life has nothing if the wife lacks household excellence. 363 names three such failings and calls each a weapon that kills the husband.

46 asks what one gains by leaving a virtuous household life for the ascetic's way. 364 calls returning to married life a fault like stoning oneself, and Mudaliar takes it as the wise telling one to give household life up. The tension holds on Mudaliar's reading; if the verse is only about remarriage after a wife's death, as Shanmuganar's gloss allows, it is narrower.
56 explains why the learned call marriage கடி, a dread; 364 opens by citing that name, and Mudaliar points back to 56.

47 puts the one who lives household life according to its nature first among all who strive; 365 puts austerity first and household life in the middle. Parimelazhagar limits 47's 'all who strive' to those in the third stage, not full renunciants, which softens the conflict.
Two ranked lists of lives side by side. Both put enjoyment of what one has in the middle and craving at the bottom, but the top changes from austerity to learning.
Both use the sprout to read what lies behind it: in 959 the sprout shows the soil as speech shows the lineage, and in 367 the paddy breeds true as a son's mind follows his father's.
169 calls the prosperity of the crooked and the ruin of the upright a thing to ponder. 368 describes that world: the worthy fallen and the base risen, the umbrella turned upside down.
788 says friendship removes distress at once, like a hand catching a slipping garment. 369 says a heart that doesn't respond so is not worth keeping alive.
The same frame, word for word in places, with two images of a love that lasts only while it is fed: the flood that ends with the rain, and the lamp that ends with the oil.

source_issues: 361: the Tamil reads கா஢யதோர், a garbled character for அரியதோர்.
362: Mudaliar glosses வழுக்கு where the verse reads வழக்கு, and reads the condition as பெறார் ஆயின் where the verse has பெறுவ ராயின்.
364: the Tamil reads இனித஧ருஉம், a garbled character; Mudaliar's gloss gives இனிது இரூஉம்.
370: Shanmuganar's field ends with the headings of the Book of Love and chapter 38 and the text of 371 with his commentary, which is repeated under 371.
